Hawkes process: self-exciting event times

Source: R/hwk.R
hwkfit.Rd

Fits a self-exciting (Hawkes) point process to event times, such as the times of shootings, burglaries or calls for service, by maximum likelihood: a background rate and, on top of it, a rise in the rate after each event that dies away with the time since. The fitted branching ratio eta is the expected number of events each event triggers; it says how much of the record is contagion rather than background.

Usage

hwkfit(
  times,
  hor,
  kernel = "exp",
  base = "const",
  per = 365.25,
  start = NULL,
  res = NULL,
  seed = NULL,
  maxit = 500
)

Arguments

times

Event times: numbers in one unit (days, say), sorted, in [0, hor]; at least 10 of them.

hor

The end of the observation window: one positive number.

kernel

The triggering kernel: one or more of "exp", "weibull" and "lomax".

base

The baseline: one or both of "const" and "cycle".

per

The length of the cycle of the "cycle" baseline, in the unit of times (365.25 for a yearly cycle in days).

start

NULL, or the starting parameters of a single kernel and baseline in the order of par (eta between 0 and 1).

res

NULL, or the resolution the times were recorded to: one positive number.

seed

NULL to draw the seed of res's spreading from R's generator, or one whole number from 0.

maxit

The most BFGS steps per start: one whole number from 1.

Value

An object of class hwkfit, a list: par, the estimates (a0 or a0 to a3 on the log scale, eta, then beta or shape and scale); se and cov, their standard errors and covariance; loglik, aic, bic; branch (eta, the mean cluster size, the stationary rate of a constant baseline and the triggered share); conv (TRUE when the gradient vanished) and iter; kernel, base, per, n, hor, jit (whether res spread the times) and times (the times fitted); and cmp, one row per kernel and baseline fitted (kernel, base, loglik, k parameters, aic, bic, eta, conv). A branching ratio above 0.99 is warned about.

Details

The intensity is $$\lambda(t) = \nu(t) + \eta \sum_{t_j < t} g(t - t_j)$$ over the window [0, hor], with a normalised kernel g: exponential ("exp", rate beta: a Markovian process), Weibull ("weibull", shape and scale) or Lomax ("lomax", the power-law kernel of seismology's modified Omori law, shape and scale, density shape / scale (1 + t / scale)^-(shape + 1)). The baseline is constant ("const", \(\nu = e^{a_0}\)) or a log-linear trend with one cycle of length per ("cycle", \(\nu(t) = \exp(a_0 + a_1 t / hor + a_2 \sin(2 \pi t / per) + a_3 \cos(2 \pi t / per))\)), whose integral is taken by Simpson's rule on steps of at most per / 16. The log-likelihood is \(\sum_i \log \lambda(t_i) - \int_0^{hor} \lambda\); it is maximised with its analytic gradient by BFGS over the baseline terms, the logit of eta (so 0 < eta < 1) and the logarithms of the kernel parameters. The exponential kernel is fitted from two starts and the better optimum kept; the others from their own start and from the exponential fit (the shape-1 member). Standard errors come from the inverse of the numerical Hessian of the analytic gradient.

Several kernels or baselines fit every combination: cmp compares them (the exponential kernel against the others is the comparison of a Markovian with a non-Markovian process) and the one with the least AIC is returned. branch holds the arithmetic of the branching process: a cluster started by one background event has 1 / (1 - eta) events on average, a constant baseline \(\nu\) gives the stationary rate \(\nu / (1 - eta)\), and the share of events that are triggered is eta (proof("hwkfit")).

Events at one instant do not excite each other: the sum runs over strictly earlier events. Times recorded to a resolution (dates, whole hours) carry ties the process never makes; res spreads each time uniformly over [t, t + res) first (cut at hor), from seed. The exponential kernel costs O(n) per likelihood, the others O(n^2).

References

Hawkes, A. G. (1971). Spectra of some self-exciting and mutually exciting point processes. Biometrika, 58(1), 83-90. doi:10.1093/biomet/58.1.83

Ozaki, T. (1979). Maximum likelihood estimation of Hawkes' self-exciting point processes. Annals of the Institute of Statistical Mathematics, 31, 145-155. doi:10.1007/BF02480272

Mohler, G. O., Short, M. B., Brantingham, P. J., Schoenberg, F. P. and Tita, G. E. (2011). Self-exciting point process modeling of crime. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 106(493), 100-108. doi:10.1198/jasa.2011.ap09546

See also

hwkres() for the residuals, hwksim() to simulate.

Examples

x <- hwksim(c(a0 = log(0.5), eta = 0.5, beta = 2), 200, seed = 1)
fit <- hwkfit(x$t, 200)
fit
#> hwkfit: 219 events in [0, 200]; exp kernel, const baseline
#>             est         se
#> a0   -0.3948088 0.13638108
#> eta   0.3874376 0.07837729
#> beta  2.4507950 0.80140193
#> branching ratio 0.3874376, mean cluster size 1.632487; log-likelihood -177.8257, AIC 361.6514
hwkfit(x$t, 200, kernel = c("exp", "lomax"))$cmp
#>   kernel  base    loglik k      aic      bic       eta conv
#> 1    exp const -177.8257 3 361.6514 371.8186 0.3874376 TRUE
#> 2  lomax const -177.8102 4 363.6204 377.1767 0.3948362 TRUE
